Attainment and Attendance in Chichester

What the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever says about the district’s secondary schools, within West Sussex and alongside Brighton and Hove. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 31, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

One of the district documents for Sussex. It sits beneath the West Sussex document, and the district summary compares all of the districts. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models of How to Pull the Right Lever. Nothing uses pupil-level records. The commentary is written to a common pattern from the figures; read it as a starting point for discussion.

Summary

Chichester’s results are among the weakest of England’s districts, on an intake less disadvantaged than England’s. Its 6 state secondary schools are in Chichester, Emsworth and Midhurst.

  • Overall results: 43.6 in Attainment 8 in 2024/25, 208th of 264 districts in England.
  • Disadvantage: 17.8% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.
  • Disadvantaged pupils average 31.0, below the national 37.8 (252nd of 264).
  • The gap between disadvantaged pupils and the rest is 15.0 points, the 56th widest of 264.

The other findings:

  • For all pupils, Chichester is 2.5 points below England. The largest pieces in the national model are prior attainment (-1.4) and the level of disadvantage (+0.9). The district’s schools take 0.8 points beyond what the model expects.
  • For disadvantaged pupils it is 4.8 points below England. The largest pieces are West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.5) and being in the South East (-1.3), and the schools take 0.3 points beyond what the model expects.
  • No district effect can be found. Once intake, West Sussex’s county effect and the schools themselves are accounted for, nothing is left that all Chichester schools share.
  • 1 of the 6 schools is above expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25. The strongest is Midhurst Rother College (+1.4); the weakest Chichester Free School (-3.1).
  • Absence was 8.0% in autumn and spring 2025/26 (8.4% a year earlier), against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25 its schools ran 0.1 points above what their intakes predict, and Chichester High School more than a point above.
  • Reduced timetables run at 1.6 times the national rate, and suspensions at 0.9 times (19.8 per 100 pupils, against 21.2).
  • Disadvantaged groups are small, 17 to 54 pupils a year per school. Every school-level figure for them moves from year to year and should be read over several years.

1 About this analysis

Chichester is a district of West Sussex, not a local authority, and that shapes what can be said:

  • The national models place schools in local authorities. The “local authority effect” in this document is West Sussex’s, shared with every school in the county.
  • What is particular to Chichester shows up in its schools’ own residuals, and in the district test of Section 6.
  • Absence and exclusions are summed over the district’s 6 schools, followed through any change of URN.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

4 What explains attainment in Chichester

The decomposition for Chichester, in Attainment 8 points. ‘Place’ is West Sussex’s effect plus the South East’s; ‘unexplained’ is what the district’s own schools add beyond everything the model accounts for.
Factor All pupils Disadvantaged Non-disadvantaged
Prior attainment (KS2) -1.38 -0.90 -1.28
Place (region and local authority) -1.20 -2.79 -1.48
Unexplained (school residual) -0.84 -0.27 -1.00
Absence -0.54 -0.58 -0.42
English as an additional language -0.24 -0.65 -0.35
Teacher workforce -0.12 -0.02 -0.11
Other model terms +0.18 -0.26 +0.16
Ofsted rating +0.67 +0.64 +0.65
Disadvantage (% FSM) +0.92 -0.32 +0.48

For all pupils, Chichester is 2.5 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • prior attainment (-1.38);
  • the level of disadvantage (+0.92);
  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-0.74);
  • Ofsted ratings (+0.67);
  • absence (-0.54);
  • being in the South East (-0.46);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-0.84), beyond what the model expects.

For disadvantaged pupils, Chichester is 4.8 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.47);
  • being in the South East (-1.32);
  • prior attainment (-0.90);
  • English as an additional language (-0.65);
  • Ofsted ratings (+0.64);
  • absence (-0.58);
  • the level of disadvantage (-0.32);
  • admissions (-0.30);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-0.27), beyond what the model expects.

The level of disadvantage counting against disadvantaged pupils is the Lever report’s most contested finding showing up locally. Across England, disadvantaged pupils do slightly better in schools with more disadvantaged pupils, once everything else is accounted for. The likely reason is that such schools organise around them, and spend pupil premium on provision that a handful of pupils cannot sustain. In Chichester, with 17 to 54 disadvantaged pupils in a year group, that is harder to do.

5 The disadvantaged gap, school by school

No Chichester school is above expectation for its non-disadvantaged pupils while more than a point below it for its disadvantaged ones. Midhurst Rother College is above expectation for both groups. The table below gives each school’s own persistent effect, from the model with a school term, which is the steadier measure.

6 Is there a Chichester effect?

The district test of the East Sussex document adds a district level to the national model, with and without each school’s own record.

None of Chichester’s district effects can be told apart from zero on either specification. The district’s results are explained by its intake, West Sussex’s county effect and its individual schools.

7 Absence

  • 8.0% absence in autumn and spring 2025/26, against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. A year earlier it was 8.4%.
  • Persistent absence is 22.2%, against 21.6% for England.
  • Against its intake, the district’s schools run 0.11 points above what their pupils’ profiles predict, on average over 2021/22 to 2024/25.
  • Chichester High School runs more than a point above its predicted absence.
  • Chichester Free School runs more than a point below its prediction.

Reduced timetables account for 0.45% of sessions, against 0.29% in England, 1.6 times the national rate. Midhurst Rother College’s rate is the highest in the district.

3 of the 6 schools are above the national average absence in 2024/25. Bringing them to it would add up to 2.1 points for all pupils, as an indication of scale.

Suspensions were 19.8 per 100 pupils in 2024/25, against 21.2 for England and 16.2 for West Sussex.

9 Questions for discussion

  1. Disadvantaged pupils. They average 31.0 in Chichester against 37.8 in England, and the district’s schools take 0.3 points for them beyond what the model expects. What do Midhurst Rother College and The Academy, Selsey, above expectation for these pupils, do that the district’s other schools could share?
  2. Attendance is a modest lever. Absence costs the district 0.5 points against England for all pupils, and Chichester High School run more than a point above what their intakes predict.
  3. Schools, not the place. There is no Chichester district effect: the differences that matter are between its schools.
  4. Practice. In Chichester, reduced timetables run at 1.6 times the national rate. These are choices made within schools, and neighbouring districts make them differently.
  5. The county. West Sussex’s own effect for disadvantaged pupils is -3.8% (131st of 151), distinguishable from zero, and it applies to every school here. The county questions in the West Sussex document apply here as well.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. District membership comes from each school’s postcode (ONS postcode directory, via postcodes.io). Absence and exclusions for the district are summed over its schools, including any predecessor or successor URNs. This document is generated from templates/district_report.qmd by R/20_district_reports.R, from data built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R and R/19_trust_effects.R. Its format is described in AREA_REPORTS.md.
